newsitem.title: ITALY: FORECAST - Lira at 1,000 vs mark seen for start 1997.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Lira at 1,000 vs mark seen for start 1997.

text.p: The lira could consolidate recent gains against the mark for the rest of this year but could start 1997 at the 1,000 level and hold around 1,010 after its return to Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism, a Reuter survey showed.
The quarterly poll of 12 leading economists saw the lira returning to the currency grid by early 1997 at the latest.
Analysts polled in the week of October 7 forecast an average lira rate of 997,08 per mark at the end of 1996, falling to 1,000 at the start of 1997 and 1.010 at the end of next year.
Martino Dolfini, economist at Chase Manhattan Bank in Milan, said he saw the lira back in the ERM at the end of November.
"Next month, preliminary consumer prices will be under 3.0 percent, and the final vote on the budget in the lower house should take place on November 18," he said.
"On Friday November 22 there could be an interest rate cut and the lira's re-entry into the ERM could follow," Dolfini said. He saw the lira's central ERM parity of 1,000 to the mark.
Alfredo Granata, economist at Banca di Roma, saw the lira's central parity between 990 and 1,010 per mark.
"Italy has been working for some time now on the lira's re-entry into the ERM, but this would logically take place after an interest rate cut which depends on the 1997 budget," he said.
Francesco Giordano, economist at San Paolo Bank in London saw the lira easing against the mark to trade around 1,010 in the last months of 1996 and 1,025 per mark in 1997.

He expected the dollar to weaken after November's U.S. presidential elections. "The lira will be pushed to the 1,025/1,050 per mark area, in which it should find its central parity," he said. He did not expect the Italian unit to rejoin the ERM until the first months of 1997.

Under the Maastricht Treaty, a country must respect the normal fluctuation margins provided for by the ERM without severe tensions for at least two years, and not devalue against the currency of another member state, in order to qualify for EMU entry.
But if Italy's admission to EMU were delayed, "Italy would have further reasons to tie the lira to the ERM in order to avoid a confidence crisis among investors," Granata said.
Giordano said the lira's average level against the mark since last October pointed to a central parity of 1,050 while the six month average pointed to a level of 1,012 per mark.

"The central parity of the Finnish markka (which entered the EMS last weekend) is based on the average in the last 18 months, but for the lira this kind of calculation would bring it in on the wrong route," Dolfini said.

Bank of Italy Governor Antonio Fazio told the Chamber of Deputies (lower house) budget commission last week "the exchange rate is not especially out of kilter". That day the lira was trading in a range of 993,50-998,30 per mark.
The lira breached the 1,000 per mark level for the first time on July 25 and touched 988.40 per mark on October 7, its highest level since July 1994.
